Week 9 sized markets and social distribution; this week asks how to **measure and manage** environmental and social externalities — noise, privacy, greenhouse gases, equity — with transparent boundaries and KPIs. Links: [Week 9](week-09.qmd) · [Glossary](glossary.qmd) · [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd).

## Summary {#summary}

**Before you go**

- Main environmental and social externalities of urban air operations (noise, privacy, greenhouse gases).
- Policy responses: pricing, operating rules, standards, mitigation, and compensation.
- Simple operational and life-cycle emissions thinking with clear boundaries.
- Privacy governance, public acceptance by use case, equity commitments, and sustainability KPIs.

**Takeaways**

- Address externalities with a mix of technology, standards, operating rules, pricing, compensation, and engagement.
- Do not “price noise” by multiplying flights by decibels above an assumed threshold.
- Privacy needs lawful purpose, necessity, proportionality, minimization, security, transparency, retention control, and accountability.
- Electric operation is not zero life-cycle emissions; GHG scopes and LCA need consistent boundaries.
- Equity commitments and KPIs need measurable outcomes, transparent funding, review, and corrective action.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Classroom numbers.** Worked examples below use round figures (noise-upgrade appraisal, privacy-control cost, carbon-value scenarios, electricity factors, public-service slot cost). They are **illustrative assumptions for learning**, not Hong Kong noise limits, CAD charges, compliance quotations, or grid-factor claims. Use sourced emissions factors and local evidence for any real inventory. Policy facts (e.g. Sandbox X / Action Plan language) stay with issuers on [Readings](#readings) / [Official status](tracker.qmd).
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of Week 10 you should be able to:

1. **Identify** major environmental and social externalities associated with urban air operations.  
2. **Compare** pricing, operating restrictions, standards, mitigation, and compensation as policy responses.  
3. **Calculate** simple operational and life-cycle greenhouse-gas indicators using transparent boundaries.  
4. **Evaluate** privacy and public-acceptance measures using necessity, proportionality, and stakeholder evidence.  
5. **Design** measurable sustainability KPIs and assess who benefits, who pays, and who bears residual impacts.

### How this week is organised

| Part | Sections | Focus |
|------|----------|--------|
| Viability & externalities | §§1–2 | Electric ≠ sustainable; noise benchmark and quieter-tech appraisal |
| Privacy & carbon screens | §§3–4 | Camera governance cost; appraisal carbon value (not a CAD tax) |
| GHG & LCA | §5 | Scopes vs LCA; electricity factor; embodied allocation |
| Acceptance & equity | §§6–7 | AiRMOUR / use-case acceptance; social licence; public-service funding |
| Close | §§8–10 | KPI design; synthesis; study checklist |

## 1. Can an LAE service be sustainable and viable?

Imagine a proposed electric-aircraft corridor near a dense urban community. The service may reduce travel time or improve delivery and public-service performance. Electricity use, vehicle manufacturing, noise, visual effects, data collection, and infrastructure still create impacts.

“Electric” does **not** automatically mean zero-emission, quiet, private, equitable, or publicly accepted. The binding constraint for a project may be noise, privacy, greenhouse-gas emissions, energy demand, or unequal distribution of benefits — often more than one at once. Week 9 asked who gains and who bears costs; this week builds the measurement tools.

**Link back to Weeks 6–9.** Week 6 availability payments and Week 8 public-service priority already encode who pays for non-commercial missions. Week 9 hedonic and distribution tables ask who bears noise and who gains access. Week 10 turns those questions into operational metrics: marginal external cost screens, privacy-control cost, Scope 2 / LCA boundaries, and KPIs with owners and corrective action.

**Connecting idea.** A contribution-positive business case (Week 9 funnel) can still fail social licence if noise, privacy, or equity residuals are unmanaged. Sustainability is a constraint set and a measurement discipline — not a marketing adjective for electric propulsion.

---

Section 1 asked whether electric propulsion equals sustainability. **Externalities** make the gap concrete. Noise and other unpriced burdens must enter cash flow or operating limits — not footnotes.

## 2. Externalities

An [**externality**](glossary.qmd#externality) is a cost or benefit that falls on other people and is not fully priced into the operator’s private costs or revenues. Noise is a common example in LAE.

An **externality** arises when an activity affects third parties and those effects are not fully reflected in the decision-maker’s private costs or benefits ([Glossary](glossary.qmd)):

| Type | Examples |
|------|----------|
| **Noise and visual effects** | Annoyance, sleep disturbance, amenity, land-use impacts |
| **Privacy and data** | Excessive collection, surveillance concerns, security risk, loss of trust |
| **Climate and energy** | Operational electricity emissions, supply-chain emissions, peak-load requirements |
| **Positive effects** | Time savings, safer inspection, emergency response, knowledge, network benefits |

**Managerial lesson:** first identify and measure the impact; then compare prevention, mitigation, pricing, compensation, and operating restrictions.

### Pricing a noise externality (economic benchmark)

Name the intermediates:

- $C^{*}_{\mathrm{noise}}$ — efficient charge per operation (economic benchmark, not a published CAD tariff)  
- $\mathrm{MEC}_{\mathrm{noise}}$ — marginal external noise cost  



$$
\begin{aligned}
C^{*}_{\mathrm{noise}}
&= \mathrm{MEC}_{\mathrm{noise}}
\end{aligned}
$$



Marginal external cost depends on exposure, time, location, number of affected people, baseline noise, event frequency, and health or amenity effects. Decibels are **logarithmic** — “decibels above a limit” should **not** automatically be multiplied by flights and a fixed monetary rate. Practical instruments may use certified noise categories, time-of-day charges, quotas, curfews, route restrictions, or performance standards. Charges should encourage quieter operations without implying that every impact can simply be paid for (Week 9 hedonic thinking informs estimation; it does not replace regulation). Vascik & Hansman and the NASA UAM noise technical paper (see [Readings](#readings)) treat noise as a **scaling constraint**, not a side note.

### Worked illustration (quieter technology)

**Illustrative assumptions:** quieter-technology upgrade costs HK\$3M; reduces expected annual noise charges, monitoring cost, and disruption by HK\$1.2M (from HK\$1.5M to HK\$0.3M).

| | Without upgrade | With upgrade |
|--|-----------------|--------------|
| Expected annual noise-related cost | HK\$1.5M | HK\$0.3M |
| Upfront cost | — | HK\$3M |
| Five-year undiscounted total | HK\$7.5M | HK\$4.5M |
| **Illustrative five-year saving** | | **HK\$3M** |

A complete appraisal should discount cash flows (Week 8 $\mathrm{NPV}$ logic with $\mathrm{CF}_{t}$) and test performance, maintenance, and demand effects. Not Hong Kong noise limits, charges, or technology quotations.

**Connecting idea.** If community acceptance binds before contribution does, a quieter-tech $\mathrm{NPV}$ that ignores mitigation cost is incomplete. Put noise cost in the cash-flow path — or in an operating restriction that cuts $K$ (Week 9 capacity) — rather than as a footnote.

---

Noise is one channel. **Privacy governance** for onboard cameras is another OPEX and trust cost — explicit, not a vague ESG haircut on revenue.

## 3. Privacy governance for onboard cameras

Cameras may support navigation, inspection, security, or evidence collection — privacy risk depends on what is captured, retained, linked, and used.

- Define a **lawful and specific purpose** before collecting personal data.  
- Test **necessity and proportionality**; consider less intrusive alternatives.  
- **Minimize** field of view, resolution, recording duration, identifiers, audio, and retention where not needed.  
- Use access controls, encryption, logs, retention limits, deletion procedures, notices, and incident response.  
- Onboard masking may be one control — it is not universally required or sufficient by itself.  

Hong Kong privacy guidance for drone cameras emphasizes avoiding excessive collection, notification, security, and responsible data handling. Course notes do not invent a specific ordinance text; verify current PCPD / regulator materials when designing a real plan.

### Privacy-control cost

- $F_{\mathrm{gov}}$ — fixed governance and system cost (PIA, design, notices, access controls, training, vendor assurance)  
- $q$ — operations (or other activity units) in the period  
- $v$ — variable processing cost per unit (secure processing, storage, communications, review, deletion)  
- $A$ — audit and incident cost  
- $C_{\mathrm{priv}}$ — annual privacy-control cost  



$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{\mathrm{priv}}
&= F_{\mathrm{gov}} + q \times v + A
\end{aligned}
$$



Cost cannot be inferred from an unsupported percentage of flight operating cost. Compare controls using privacy effectiveness, safety compatibility, reliability, and total cost.

**Illustrative assumptions:** 50,000 operations/year; fixed privacy-system and governance cost HK\$600k/year (base design); set $A = 0$ in the teaching screen.

| | Lower variable cost | Higher-assurance design |
|--|---------------------|-------------------------|
| Processing | HK\$4/op → HK\$200k | HK\$8/op → HK\$400k |
| Fixed | HK\$600k | HK\$1M |
| **Annual cost** | **HK\$800k** | **HK\$1.4M** |

The more expensive design is justified only if additional controls materially improve privacy, security, or operational assurance. Not a compliance quotation or claim that either design is legally sufficient.

Privacy is operational; carbon often enters as appraisal. **Carbon cost scenarios** are teaching aids — **not** a claimed CAD aviation tax — unless an issuer rule applies.

## 4. Carbon cost scenarios (appraisal aid — not a claimed CAD tax)

A carbon value can support investment appraisal. **Illustrative assumptions:** 50,000 operations/year; carbon value HK\$1 per kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$.

| Intensity | Annual emissions | Annual carbon cost |
|-----------|------------------|--------------------|
| 40 kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$/operation | $50{,}000 \times 40 = 2{,}000{,}000$ kg | **HK\$2M** |
| 10 kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$/operation | $50{,}000 \times 10 = 500{,}000$ kg | **HK\$0.5M** |

This is **not** a claim that CAD imposes such a tax. Emissions factors and boundaries must be sourced.

**Connecting idea.** Treat the carbon value as an **appraisal dial** (like Week 8’s illustrative peak charge), not as an invented Hong Kong aviation carbon levy. If a real carbon price or reporting rule applies, cite the issuer.

A carbon value needs an inventory. **GHG scopes and LCA** answer different boundary questions — do not add them into one misleading total.

## 5. GHG inventory and life-cycle assessment





Corporate GHG **scopes** and product **life-cycle assessment (LCA)** answer related but different questions:

| Concept | Focus |
|---------|--------|
| **Scope 1** | Direct emissions from sources owned or controlled by the reporting organization |
| **Scope 2** | Indirect emissions associated with purchased electricity, steam, heat, or cooling |
| **Scope 3** | Other indirect value-chain emissions (e.g. aircraft, batteries, infrastructure, maintenance, end-of-life) |
| [**LCA**](glossary.qmd#lca) | Environmental impacts of a defined product or service across a specified life cycle and functional unit |

An electric aircraft may have zero in-flight exhaust emissions while still having Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions. Corporate scopes should not simply be added without checking boundaries and double counting. Stolaroff et al. and Kasliwal et al. ([Readings](#readings)) illustrate why delivery-drone and VTOL sustainability claims depend on grid intensity, utilization, and the comparison mode — not on “electric” alone.

### Electricity-related (operational) emissions

- $E_{\mathrm{kWh}}$ — electricity consumed per operation (kWh), including charging losses if inside the boundary  
- $f_{\mathrm{grid}}$ — electricity emissions factor (e.g. kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$/kWh)  
- $e_{\mathrm{op}}$ — operational electricity-related emissions per operation  



$$
\begin{aligned}
e_{\mathrm{op}}
&= E_{\mathrm{kWh}} \times f_{\mathrm{grid}}
\end{aligned}
$$



Match units carefully. Include charging losses and relevant facility energy if they fall within the boundary. Distinguish location-based grid factors from market-based contractual claims where applicable. Compare modes using a consistent functional unit (passenger-km, tonne-km, or completed mission).

**Assumption (illustrative):** $E_{\mathrm{kWh}} = 50$.

| Factor $f_{\mathrm{grid}}$ | Result $e_{\mathrm{op}}$ |
|--------|--------|
| 0.8 kg/kWh | **40 kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$/operation** |
| 0.2 kg/kWh | **10 kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$/operation** |

Electricity source matters — these figures alone do not establish whether the service outperforms another transport mode. Occupancy, distance, infrastructure, and life-cycle emissions also matter. Use current, sourced factors for an actual inventory.

### Life-cycle emissions per functional unit

- $E_{\mathrm{v}}, E_{\mathrm{b}}, E_{\mathrm{i}}, E_{\mathrm{o}}, E_{\mathrm{e}}$ — vehicle, battery, infrastructure, operations, and end-of-life emissions in the chosen boundary  
- $U$ — lifetime functional units (passenger-km, tonne-km, missions, …)  
- $e_{\mathrm{FU}}$ — life-cycle emissions per functional unit  



$$
\begin{aligned}
e_{\mathrm{FU}}
&= \frac{E_{\mathrm{v}} + E_{\mathrm{b}} + E_{\mathrm{i}} + E_{\mathrm{o}} + E_{\mathrm{e}}}{U}
\end{aligned}
$$



State lifetime, utilization, replacement cycles, occupancy or payload, system boundary, and allocation method. Scope 3 is **not** a universal fixed percentage of total emissions. Compare alternatives using the **same** boundary and functional unit.

**Illustrative assumptions:** embodied aircraft, battery, and infrastructure emissions allocated at 12 kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$ per operation (a teaching allocation of embodied mass into a per-operation screen — not a published factor).

| | Higher-carbon electricity | Lower-carbon electricity |
|--|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| Electricity | 40 kg | 10 kg |
| Allocated embodied | 12 kg | 12 kg |
| **Total** | **52 kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$/operation** | **22 kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$/operation** |

Decarbonizing electricity reduces operational emissions; embodied emissions remain sensitive to lifetime use and replacement assumptions. Not a comparative claim about jets or sustainable aviation fuel.

**Connecting idea.** Do not add [Scope 1+2+3](glossary.qmd#ghg-scopes) totals to an LCA total without a boundary map — that is the GHG analogue of Week 9’s double-counted barrier haircuts.

---

Inventories measure burdens. **Public acceptance by use case** asks whose consent matters — traveller choice share is not the same as resident social licence under the route.

## 6. Public acceptance by use case

**AiRMOUR** examined sustainable UAM through the lens of emergency medical services while also considering other applications ([Glossary · AiRMOUR](glossary.qmd) — closed EU research action; **not** a company or OEM brand). Acceptance may vary with perceived public benefit, urgency, safety, noise, privacy, fairness, trust, location, and available alternatives. Urgent medical applications may receive stronger support than some non-urgent applications — acceptance is **not** automatic or perfectly divided into two groups. Infrastructure maintenance, surveying, and environmental monitoring may also be viewed favourably in some contexts.

Local engagement and evidence are necessary before transferring European findings to Hong Kong. **Managerial lesson:** segment by use case and affected stakeholder; test assumptions rather than assigning universal acceptance scores (Week 9 distribution theme; EASA societal-acceptance study listed with Week 4 / Week 9 readings).

**Connecting idea.** Choice share $s$ in the Week 9 funnel is not the same as community acceptance of overflights. A high $s$ among travellers can coexist with low social licence among residents under the route — model both.

---

Acceptance and equity meet funding. **Social licence and public-service commitments** need a payable source when priority flights displace commercial contribution.

## 7. Equity, social licence, and funding commitments

[**Social licence**](glossary.qmd#social-license) refers to continuing acceptance and trust among affected communities and stakeholders. It complements, but does **not** replace, legal approval. Ask who receives time savings, service improvements, employment, and business opportunities — and who bears noise, privacy, safety, land-use, and fiscal costs. Consider affordability, accessibility, geographic coverage, consultation, complaints, and remedies. Acceptance may change over time and cannot be purchased by one symbolic public-service commitment.

**Managerial lesson:** build legitimacy through performance, transparency, participation, mitigation, and fair distribution of benefits and costs.

### Funding a public-service commitment

- $Q_{C}, m_{C}$ — commercial quantity and contribution margin per unit  
- $P_{\mathrm{PS}}$ — public-service payment (procurement, availability payment, or other transparent source)  
- $Q_{P}, c_{P}$ — public-service quantity and incremental cost per unit  
- $F$ — fixed cost allocated to the period  
- $\Pi_{\mathrm{net}}$ — net contribution after the commitment  



$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi_{\mathrm{net}}
&= Q_{C}\, m_{C} + P_{\mathrm{PS}} - Q_{P}\, c_{P} - F
\end{aligned}
$$



Funding may come from commercial cross-subsidy, public procurement, availability payment (Week 6), philanthropy, or another transparent source. Specify eligibility, service level, opportunity cost, accountability, and long-term affordability.

**Assumptions (illustrative):** 100 daily slots; commercial contribution HK\$400/flight; public-service incremental cost HK\$100/flight; $P_{\mathrm{PS}} = 0$ and $F$ omitted in the teaching screen below.

| | All commercial | Twenty priority slots |
|--|----------------|----------------------|
| Commercial contribution | $100 \times 400$ = HK\$40,000 | $80 \times 400$ = HK\$32,000 |
| Public-service cost | — | $20 \times 100$ = HK\$2,000 |
| **Net before fixed cost** | **HK\$40,000/day** | **HK\$30,000/day** |
| Opportunity cost vs all-commercial | — | HK\$10,000/day |

The commitment has a measurable cost. Whether it is justified — and who should fund it — requires public-value and distributional assessment. No claim that the commitment secures approval or acceptance.

Keep **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X** when citing trial programmes; Action Plan language and Sandbox X commitments stay with the 2025 Policy Address / Official status issuers ([Readings](#readings)). Do not claim cross-boundary corridors as day-to-day operating service.

**Connecting idea.** Week 8’s priority rules decide *who flies*; this week’s $\Pi_{\mathrm{net}}$ decides *who pays* when priority displaces commercial contribution. Write both down before promising “twenty free public-service flights.”

---

Commitments need metrics. [**Sustainability KPI**](glossary.qmd#kpi) design** ties noise, privacy, carbon, and equity to boundaries, owners, and corrective action — then the tool map closes the loop.

## 8. Sustainability KPI design

| Area | Example KPI | Boundary or denominator |
|------|-------------|-------------------------|
| Noise | Population-weighted exposure | Route, period, and noise metric |
| Climate | kg $\mathrm{CO}_{2}\mathrm{e}$ / passenger-km | Life-cycle boundary and occupancy |
| Privacy | Personal-data incidents | Operations and severity |
| Equity | Service availability by area | Population, need, and affordability |
| Governance | Complaints resolved on time | Defined process and deadline |

Define baseline, target, measurement method, frequency, owner, assurance, and corrective action. There is **no** universal CAD or investor requirement that mandates a fixed trio of ratios invented in class. A KPI tracks performance — it does not by itself prove profitability or social acceptance.

**Mitigation scorecard (classroom):** for each material impact (noise, privacy, climate, equity), record measure, KPI, and payer. Do **not** assume a 60 dB limit or a fixed number of free public-service flights. Define thresholds from evidence, regulation, operating context, and stakeholder agreement.

### One-page tool map (from externality to KPI)

| Step | Ask | Output |
|------|-----|--------|
| 1 | Which externalities bind (noise, privacy, climate, equity)? | Impact list with affected parties |
| 2 | What is $\mathrm{MEC}_{\mathrm{noise}}$ vs practical instrument? | Charge / quota / curfew / standard screen |
| 3 | Privacy: purpose, necessity, minimization — and $C_{\mathrm{priv}}$? | Control design + cost channel |
| 4 | Carbon value for appraisal only — or a real priced rule? | Attribution discipline (not invented CAD tax) |
| 5 | $e_{\mathrm{op}} = E_{\mathrm{kWh}} \times f_{\mathrm{grid}}$ with sourced $f_{\mathrm{grid}}$? | Scope 2 operational screen |
| 6 | Same boundary for $e_{\mathrm{FU}}$ vs comparator mode? | LCA screen without double counting |
| 7 | Acceptance by **use case** and stakeholder — not one score? | Segmented acceptance hypothesis |
| 8 | $\Pi_{\mathrm{net}}$ with explicit $P_{\mathrm{PS}}$ and opportunity cost? | Funded public-service commitment |
| 9 | KPI: baseline, owner, frequency, corrective action? | Mitigation scorecard row |
| 10 | Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X; Policy Address / Action Plan cited to issuer only | Fact discipline |

Pull the thread: externalities → privacy → appraisal carbon → GHG/LCA boundaries → acceptance vs licence → funded equity → KPIs — electric remains necessary but not sufficient.

## 9. Putting Week 10 together

Externalities should be measured and addressed through a mix of technology, standards, operating rules, pricing, compensation, and engagement. Noise cannot be priced reliably by multiplying flights by decibels above an assumed threshold. Privacy governance requires lawful purpose, necessity, proportionality, minimization, security, transparency, retention control, and accountability. Corporate GHG scopes and LCA need clear, consistent boundaries — **electric operation does not imply zero life-cycle emissions**. Public acceptance varies across use cases and stakeholders. Equity commitments and KPIs need measurable outcomes, transparent funding, review, and corrective action.

The short checklist is in [Summary](#summary) above.

---

## 10. Study checklist

1. State why “electric” does not imply zero life-cycle emissions, quietness, privacy, or equity.  
2. Define an externality; give one negative and one positive LAE example.  
3. Write $C^{*}_{\mathrm{noise}} = \mathrm{MEC}_{\mathrm{noise}}$; say why “flights × dB above limit × \$” is wrong.  
4. Appraise a quieter-tech upgrade with discounted cash flows — label figures illustrative.  
5. Compute $C_{\mathrm{priv}} = F_{\mathrm{gov}} + q v + A$ for two assurance levels.  
6. Separate an appraisal carbon dial from any claimed CAD carbon tax.  
7. Compute $e_{\mathrm{op}}$ for two grid factors; state units and boundary.  
8. Compute $e_{\mathrm{FU}}$; list what must be held constant when comparing modes.  
9. Explain AiRMOUR as a closed EU research action — not an OEM brand; segment acceptance by use case.  
10. Compute $\Pi_{\mathrm{net}}$ for a public-service slot commitment; name who pays.  
11. Fill one mitigation-scorecard row (measure, KPI, payer) without inventing a 60 dB rule.  
12. Keep **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**; cite 2025 Policy Address Action Plan / Sandbox X language only to the issuer.

## Readings {#readings}

### Main references

- [2025 Policy Address, paras. 153–157](https://www.policyaddress.gov.hk/2025/en/p153.html) — HKSAR. Sandbox X and the commitment to formulate an Action Plan.

  ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" title="官方中英文本 · Official English and Chinese"}
  English: “We will formulate the Action Plan on Developing Low-Altitude Economy to advance Hong Kong as a major hub for low-altitude applications through institutional innovations and technological breakthroughs.” ([source](https://www.policyaddress.gov.hk/2025/en/p153.html))

  [「我們會制訂「發展低空經濟規劃行動綱領」，透過制度創新與技術突破，令香港成為低空創新應用的核心樞紐」]{lang="zh-Hant"} ([source](https://www.policyaddress.gov.hk/2025/tc/p153.html))

  English: “We will regularise the operation of more mature application scenarios, and roll out the advanced low-altitude economy \"Regulatory Sandbox X \" pilot projects to cover application scenarios that are technically more complex, such as cross-boundary routes and passenger-carrying, low-altitude aircraft.” ([source](https://www.policyaddress.gov.hk/2025/en/p156.html))

  [「較成熟的應用場景將恆常化運行，並推出進階版低空經濟「監管沙盒X」試點項目，涵蓋跨境路線、低空載人飛行器等技術複雜度較高的應用場景。」]{lang="zh-Hant"} ([source](https://www.policyaddress.gov.hk/2025/tc/p156.html))
  :::
